content: Urgent care refers to the provision of outpatient medical services in facilities specifically designed to handle unscheduled, walk-in patients who require immediate attention for non-life-threatening conditions. These centers are distinct from hospital emergency departments, which operate 24/7 and are equipped to manage critical, life-threatening emergencies. Urgent care centers typically operate on a more limited schedule and are intended for conditions that do not necessitate the resources of a full emergency room. The concept of urgent care began in the 1970s, and the sector has since grown significantly, with approximately 17,000 centers now in operation. Many of these facilities were established by entrepreneurial physicians responding to the public's demand for convenient, unscheduled medical care. Others have been developed by hospital systems aiming to attract patients. The growth of urgent care centers has been driven in part by the cost savings they offer compared to hospital emergency departments. Managed care organizations (MCOs) often encourage their members to utilize urgent care services as a cost-effective alternative. Urgent care centers differ from other ambulatory healthcare facilities in several ways. Emergency departments, for example, are located within hospitals and are designed to handle true medical emergencies, such as heart attacks, severe trauma from motor vehicle accidents, or suicide attempts. These departments are staffed by physicians with specialized training or board certification in emergency medicine and have access to critical care units and surgical facilities. In contrast, urgent care centers are not equipped to manage such high-acuity cases. Primary care offices with extended hours may offer evening and weekend appointments, but unless they accept walk-in patients, provide on-site X-ray services, and treat conditions like simple fractures and lacerations, they do not meet the criteria for urgent care centers. Similarly, walk-in primary care offices that lack expanded services and after-hours care are not classified as urgent care facilities. Retail-based clinics, which began appearing in 2004, are another type of ambulatory care facility. These clinics are typically located within retail stores with pharmacies and are staffed by nurse practitioners or physician assistants. While they offer convenience and transparent pricing, they are not considered true urgent care centers due to their limited scope of services and the absence of on-site physicians and X-ray capabilities. Concerns about potential conflicts of interest, such as incentives to overprescribe medications, remain unresolved in these settings. The urgent care industry has become increasingly organized, with professional associations such as the Urgent Care Association of America (UCAOA), the American Academy of Urgent Care Medicine (AAUCM), and the National Association for Ambulatory Urgent Care (NAFAC) holding annual conventions and conferences. These organizations are working toward the recognition of urgent care as a distinct medical specialty, with dedicated training programs and fellowships. In 2006, the UCAOA sponsored the first fellowship training program in urgent care medicine in collaboration with the Department of Family Medicine at University Hospitals of Cleveland and the Case School of Medicine. This program provides physicians with training in adult and pediatric emergencies, wound care, occupational medicine, urgent care procedures, and the business aspects of running an urgent care center. A second fellowship program was established in 2007 at the University of Illinois. These one-year fellowships are open to graduates of accredited Family Medicine and Med/Peds residency programs. The American Medical Association has approved the designation Urgent Care Medicine (UCM) for physicians specializing in this field. Services provided in urgent care centers can be coded using specific designations, such as S9083 (global fee for urgent care centers) and S9088 (services rendered in an urgent care center). The UCAOA offers advanced coding workshops to help providers and coders navigate the complexities of urgent care billing. The urgent care industry has also seen the development of specialized services and supporting industries. For example, point-of-care medication dispensing allows patients to receive their prescriptions before leaving the clinic. Practice management software tailored to urgent care operations has been developed, and group purchasing organizations (GPOs) have been formed to enable centers to negotiate better pricing on supplies and services. Additionally, malpractice insurance policies specific to urgent care centers have emerged, reflecting the lower risk profile of these facilities compared to hospital emergency departments. These policies often include features such as no-cost tail coverage, rapid approval of new providers, and lower premiums. The industry is supported by professional publications, such as the Journal of Urgent Care Medicine (JUCM), the official publication of the UCAOA, and Urgent Care, published by the American Academy of Urgent Care Medicine. These journals provide valuable resources for physicians, physician assistants, and nurse practitioners working in the field. In summary, urgent care centers have become an essential component of the healthcare system, offering accessible, cost-effective care for non-emergency conditions. The industry continues to evolve, with advancements in training, coding, and supporting services contributing to its growth and professionalization.
